result.question: Opinionated project scaffolding best practices for Python and TypeScript (2025-2026), to design what a coding-agent harness should generate out of the box. Sub-lanes: (1) Python: current consensus stack for a new project — uv vs poetry/pip, ruff (lint+format) config people actually ship, pyright vs mypy strictness, src/ layout vs flat, pyproject.toml-only, pytest conventions, pre-commit; recommended module/file size and structure norms. (2) TypeScript: strict tsconfig baseline (which flags), Biome vs ESLint+Prettier adoption state, vitest as default test runner, folder-by-feature vs folder-by-type, barrel-file (index.ts re-export) pros/cons and current guidance, pnpm/monorepo defaults. (3) Out-of-box usability of dev tools: what makes scaffolds like create-vite / create-next-app / cookiecutter / copier succeed — defaults-over-configuration philosophy, zero-config trend, template maintenance/drift problems, and how opinionated starters keep generated projects consistent over time.
result.summary: For a coding-agent harness generating new projects in 2025-2026, the evidence converges on a clear opinionated core. Python: scaffold with uv (single Rust binary that replaces pip/venv/virtualenv/pip-tools/pyenv/Poetry, auto-manages the venv, ~8-10x faster cold / 80-115x warm than pip) + Ruff (one tool for lint AND format, 800-900+ consolidated rules, >99.9% Black-compatible formatter), a src/ layout, and a single pyproject.toml holding the entire toolchain's config. TypeScript: set tsconfig strict:true (the umbrella toggle — do not re-enumerate its sub-flags) plus a few complementary non-family flags, and default the test runner to Vitest (zero-config ESM/TS/JSX) over Jest. The overriding design lesson for scaffolds themselves is that template drift is the real maintenance problem — tools like cruft/copier exist to keep generated projects synchronized with their upstream template, so a generator must plan for ongoing update, not one-time creation. Two important gaps survived verification unresolved and should NOT be hardcoded: the Python type-checker choice (mypy vs pyright, and Astral's ty) and the TS linter/formatter choice (Biome vs ESLint+Prettier).

findings.claim: For new Python projects in 2025-2026, uv (from Astral) is the consensus default for dependency management, environment creation, and locking — a single Rust binary positioned to replace pip, pip-tools, virtualenv, pyenv, and Poetry. It auto-manages the virtualenv (no manual venv handling), runs ~8-10x faster cold-cache and 80-115x warm-cache than pip, and migrating existing Poetry projects is treated as optional rather than urgent (Poetry 2.4.x remains actively maintained and viable). For a harness, `uv init` is the default project bootstrap.
findings.evidence: Four separate blog sources each passed 3-0 adversarial verification, and all are backstopped by Astral's primary docs, which state verbatim: 'A single tool to replace pip, pip-tools, pipx, poetry, pyenv, twine, virtualenv, and more.' Auto-venv confirmed by Astral docs + Real Python ('uv add ... automatically creates a virtual environment and manages it for you'). The 10-100x range is honest (spans cold and warm scenarios), independently reproduced (~8x JupyterLab, 11.3x Techplained; venv creation 0.045s vs pip 6.1s). uv reached ~75M monthly PyPI downloads, surpassing Poetry ~April 2026. Adversarial search for downsides surfaced only edge-case caveats (Windows static-distro/OpenSSL, missing dependency upper bounds) — even the most critical source concluded uv is production-fine as of Feb 2026.

findings.claim: A key design rationale for the modern Python stack is single-vendor integration: uv and Ruff (and Astral's in-progress type checker, ty) come from the same company and share the pyproject.toml config surface ([tool.uv], [tool.ruff], [tool.ty]), reducing tool-boundary friction and maintenance overhead.
findings.evidence: Confirmed via the astral-sh GitHub org and docs.astral.sh: all tools read config from their [tool.*] table in pyproject.toml (identical pattern). Simon Willison and Talk Python corroborate Astral as the vendor behind uv/ruff/ty; OpenAI's March 2026 acquisition of Astral reinforces the single-vendor framing. Caveat carried forward: ty is still beta (Dec 2025), so 'seamlessly' is slightly generous, and the tools are complementary rather than functionally overlapping.

findings.claim: Ruff is the consensus single tool for BOTH linting and formatting in new Python projects, consolidating 800-900+ rules from flake8 (plus dozens of plugins), isort, pyupgrade, pydocstyle, and bandit into one Rust binary. Its formatter (`ruff format`) is a drop-in Black replacement, >99.9% line-identical on Black-formatted code, and it runs 10-100x faster than the tools it replaces.
findings.evidence: Every sub-claim confirmed against Astral's primary docs/FAQ: '900+' built-in rules; native rules from Flake8/isort/pyupgrade/pydocstyle/Bandit; formatter 'designed to be a drop-in replacement for Black' with '>99.9% of lines formatted identically' on Django/Zulip; '10-100x faster than existing linters and formatters.' Ruff was named the most-admired developer tool overall in the Stack Overflow 2025 survey; FastAPI/Pandas/SciPy/Airflow have migrated. Nuance (compression, not misrepresentation): the >99.9% figure measures already-Black-formatted code; non-Black code diverges slightly more (end-of-line comments, long asserts).

findings.claim: The advocated Python project structure is a src/ layout (src/<package>/, tests/, data/) over a flat layout. The canonical PyPA rationale: because src/ is not on sys.path, it forces installing the package before tests run and prevents accidental imports of the in-development working tree; it also improves packaging and type-checker configuration. A harness should scaffold src/ by default.
findings.evidence: The PyPA Packaging User Guide (primary) states verbatim both mechanisms: 'The src layout requires installation of the project to be able to run its code' and 'helps prevent accidental usage of the in-development copy of the code.' Corroborated by Real Python and pyOpenSci. The existing src-vs-flat debate contests only whether src is strictly NECESSARY and notes one con (a CLI can't run directly from the source tree) — it does not dispute the stated mechanism, so it is orthogonal. Flat layout remains acceptable for trivial single-file scripts.

findings.claim: pyproject.toml should be the single configuration file for the entire Python toolchain — uv ([tool.uv]), Ruff ([tool.ruff]), mypy ([tool.mypy]), pytest ([tool.pytest.ini_options]), coverage ([tool.coverage.*]), and build/[project] metadata (PEP 621/518) all live there — replacing setup.cfg, setup.py, .flake8, and mypy.ini.
findings.evidence: Corroborated by each tool's primary docs: mypy supports [tool.mypy] since 0.900; uv recommends keeping config in pyproject.toml (uv.toml optional); Ruff, pytest, coverage.py and PEP 621 build metadata all support it. The only mypy limitation (no standalone mypy.toml, issue #18617) is irrelevant to the claim. .flake8 is dropped rather than migrated because the modern stack uses Ruff, which replaces flake8. Originating source is a blog, but this is mainstream consensus, not an extraordinary claim.

findings.claim: The TypeScript baseline is tsconfig `strict: true` — a single umbrella toggle equivalent to enabling all strict-mode-family flags (noImplicitAny, strictNullChecks, strictFunctionTypes, strictBindCallApply, strictPropertyInitialization, noImplicitThis, alwaysStrict, useUnknownInCatchVariables). Re-enumerating those sub-flags on top of strict is redundant and NOT recommended. Opinionated guides then layer complementary NON-family flags for maximum correctness: noUncheckedIndexedAccess, exactOptionalPropertyTypes, noUnusedLocals, noUnusedParameters, forceConsistentCasingInFileNames.
findings.evidence: Official TS docs (primary): 'Turning this on is equivalent to enabling all of the strict mode family options ... enables a wide range of type checking behavior that results in stronger guarantees of program correctness.' The opinionated guide (last modified 2026-03-17) frames strict + complementary flags as yielding 'maximum correctness and minimal mystery errors.' Importantly, a sibling claim asserting you should ALSO explicitly declare individual sub-flags was REFUTED 0-3 — the umbrella flag is sufficient, so a harness should not scaffold redundant sub-flag enumeration. Complementary flags (noUncheckedIndexedAccess, exactOptionalPropertyTypes) are correctly NOT part of the strict family and must be added explicitly if desired.

findings.claim: Vitest is the modern default TypeScript test runner: it supports ESM, TypeScript, and JSX with zero configuration, whereas Jest still treats ESM as a 'second-class citizen' (experimental, requiring --experimental-vm-modules plus transform config and type:module). Caveat for harness design: Vitest's 'TypeScript support' means esbuild type-stripping to RUN .ts files, not type-checking — a separate `tsc --noEmit` (or ty/mypy analog) step is still needed.
findings.evidence: Source states verbatim 'Vitest supports ESM, TypeScript, and JSX with zero configuration' and calls Jest ESM 'a second class citizen even today.' The technical comparison is corroborated by Jest's OWN docs, which confirm ESM support is still experimental and requires the --experimental-vm-modules flag. Confidence is high on the zero-config FACT (primary-doc corroborated); the normative 'superior/default' framing is one educator's opinion, though it reflects broad 2025-2026 sentiment.

findings.claim: The dominant maintenance problem for opinionated scaffolds is TEMPLATE DRIFT: generators like cookiecutter create projects by copy-paste, leaving boilerplate with no easy path to absorb upstream template changes. Tools like cruft (and copier) exist specifically to keep generated projects synchronized — `cruft update` re-syncs to the latest template and `cruft check` fails CI on drift. The design implication for a project-generating harness: treat generation as an ongoing update relationship, not a one-time emission.
findings.evidence: cruft's 'Why Create cruft?' section confirms the framing verbatim: scaffolding tools 'encouraged more code to be copied and pasted!' leaving 'hundreds of projects that contained copy-and-pasted code with no easy way to update them.' The sync half is documented: `cruft update` 'automates the process of updating code to match the latest version of a template' and `cruft check` validates drift in CI. Independent sources (Astronomer, MLOps Coding Course, python-basics-tutorial) all use the exact term 'template drift.' Non-refuting nuance: some teams now prefer copier for the same problem.

result.caveats:
SOURCE QUALITY: The confirmed claims lean heavily on blogs, but each survived 3-0 verification only because it was backstopped by PRIMARY sources — Astral docs (uv/ruff/ty), typescriptlang.org, PyPA packaging guide, Jest official docs, mypy/pytest/coverage docs. Blog-only opinion words ('consensus', 'superior', 'the config to choose') carry less weight than the underlying tool facts.

DO NOT HARDCODE (verification says otherwise): (1) The full 'uv + Ruff + Ty + Polars' stack claim was REFUTED 0-3 — ty is still beta (Dec 2025) and is NOT confirmed as a default; Polars is not a general-project dependency. (2) The Python type-checker recommendation is UNRESOLVED — both claims proposing a mypy-in-CI + pyright-in-editor split were refuted 0-3, so there is no verified recommendation on which type checker or what strictness to scaffold. (3) The TS linter/formatter choice is UNRESOLVED — both Biome-vs-ESLint+Prettier claims were refuted, so neither a 'use Biome' nor a 'stick with ESLint+Prettier' verdict is supported by the evidence. (4) A claim to enumerate individual tsconfig strict sub-flags on top of `strict:true` was refuted — the umbrella flag suffices.

TIME-SENSITIVITY: Fast-moving space. uv surpassed Poetry in downloads ~April 2026; OpenAI acquired Astral ~March 2026; ty reached beta Dec 2025. One source's Poetry version was imprecise (2.4.0 vs actual 2.4.1, May 2026). The Poetry-recommending source (laszlo.substack) is from 2023 and predates the uv shift — it supports 'src/ layout' and 'pyproject.toml as single config' but its Poetry recommendation is superseded. Recommendations are valid for 2025-2026 and will continue shifting.

COVERAGE GAPS: Several sub-lanes of the research question produced NO confirmed claims at all (see open questions) — treat their absence as 'not evidenced here', not 'no consensus exists'.
openQuestions: Python type-checker default: mypy vs pyright vs Astral's ty, and what strictness level — no verified recommendation survived (both proposed split-strategies were refuted 0-3, and the ty-in-stack claim was refuted). A harness needs a decision here that this research did not settle.

TypeScript linter/formatter default: Biome vs ESLint+Prettier — unresolved. Both Biome claims (the '97% of ESLint rules / no plugins' state-of-readiness claim and the 'not yet ready to replace' verdict) were refuted, leaving no evidenced default either way.

Entirely unevidenced sub-lanes: pnpm and monorepo defaults; TS folder-by-feature vs folder-by-type; barrel-file (index.ts re-export) pros/cons and current guidance. No confirmed claims were produced for any of these despite being in scope.
Python testing/quality conventions: pytest layout conventions, pre-commit adoption norms, and recommended module/file-size limits — no confirmed claims. Needs a separate targeted pass.

The defaults-over-configuration / zero-config success factors of create-vite and create-next-app specifically: only the drift/synchronization angle (cruft/copier) was confirmed; the direct evidence on WHY create-vite/create-next-app succeed as opinionated starters was not established.

refuted.claim: The recommended 2026 Python project stack is uv (install/env/deps/locking/running) + Ruff (lint+format) + Ty (type checking) + Polars (dataframes), replacing the older fragmented pyenv+pip+venv+pip-tools/Poetry+Black+isort+Flake8+mypy+pandas approach.
The recommended type-checking baseline splits by context: mypy in strict mode is the standard for CI, while pyright (via Pylance) is recommended for real-time IDE feedback.
The recommended 2026 type-checking strategy is split: pyright in the editor and mypy in CI (rather than choosing one exclusively).
The src/ layout plus pyproject.toml (PEP 621) are now the standard project structure, replacing setup.py and root-level imports; src/ prevents accidental root-level imports.

For a new TypeScript project's tsconfig, the recommended baseline is strict mode plus explicitly declaring the individual strict sub-flags (noImplicitAny, strictNullChecks, strictPropertyInitialization) rather than relying only on the strict umbrella flag.

Biome (as of early 2025) natively implements about 97% of ESLint's rules, but by design will not port all of them, and its lack of a plugin system means some project-specific-but-essential rules are unavailable.

The author's verdict is that Biome is not yet ready to fully replace ESLint+Prettier: ESLint and Prettier remain the top choice for most projects, while Biome is a good alternative for small projects.
